ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, in the Cartesian coordinate system $xOy$, the rectangle $ABCD$ has its side $AB$ on the $x$-axis, with $AB=3$ and $AD=2$. The line passing through point $C$ and described by $y=x-2$ intersects the $x$-axis and $y$-axis at points $E$ and $F$, respectively. The question is whether there exists a point $P$ on the line $y=x-2$ such that $\triangle PDC$ is an isosceles right-angled triangle. Determine the coordinates of point $P$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} There exists.
\\
$\because \triangle EBC$ is an isosceles right-angled triangle,\\
$\therefore \angle CEB=\angle ECB=45^\circ$,\\
Also, $\because DC\parallel AB$,\\
$\therefore \angle DCE=\angle CEB=45^\circ$,\\
$\therefore \triangle PDC$ can only be an isosceles right-angled triangle with $P$ and $D$ as the right-angled vertices.\\
As shown in the figure, (1) when $\angle D=90^\circ$, extend $DA$ to intersect the line $y=x-2$ at point $P_1$,\\
$\because$ the coordinates of point $D$ are $(1, 2)$,\\
$\therefore$ the $x$-coordinate of point $P_1$ is 1,\\
Substituting $x=1$ into $y=x-2$ gives, $y=-1$,\\
$\therefore$ the point $P_1(1, -1)$;\\
(2) when $\angle DPC=90^\circ$, draw the perpendicular bisector of $DC$ to intersect the line $y=x-2$ at point $P_2$,\\
Therefore, the $x$-coordinate of point $P_2$ is $\frac{1+4}{2}=\frac{5}{2}$,\\
Substituting $x=\frac{5}{2}$ into $y=x-2$ gives, $y=\frac{1}{2}$,\\
Therefore, the point $P_2\left(\frac{5}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)$,\\
In summary, the coordinates of the suitable point $P$ are \boxed{(1, -1)} or \boxed{\left(\frac{5}{2}, \frac{1}{2}\right)}.

Determine whether there exists a point $P$ on the line $y=x-2$ such that $\triangle PDC$ is an isosceles right-angled triangle, and if so, find the coordinates of point $P$.
ready1_open_rewrite.expected_answer: There exists such a point. Since $\triangle EBC$ is an isosceles right-angled triangle, $\angle CEB=\angle ECB=45^\circ$. Also, because $DC\parallel AB$, $\angle DCE=\angle CEB=45^\circ$. Therefore, $\triangle PDC$ can only be an isosceles right-angled triangle with either $D$ or $P$ as the right-angle vertex. (1) When the right angle is at $D$, extend $DA$ to intersect the line $y=x-2$ at point $P_1$. Since the coordinates of point $D$ are $(1,2)$, the $x$-coordinate of $P_1$ is $1$. Substituting $x=1$ into $y=x-2$ gives $y=-1$, so $P_1=(1,-1)$. (2) When $\angle DPC=90^\circ$, the point $P_2$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $DC$ and on the line $y=x-2$. Thus the $x$-coordinate of $P_2$ is $\frac{1+4}{2}=\frac{5}{2}$. Substituting $x=\frac{5}{2}$ into $y=x-2$ gives $y=\frac{1}{2}$, so $P_2=\left(\frac{5}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right)$. Therefore, the suitable coordinates of $P$ are $(1,-1)$ or $\left(\frac{5}{2},\frac{1}{2}\right)$.
